source.title: A New Medicare Option for Weight Loss Drugs: What Older Americans Should Know

payload.value: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced on May 6, 2026, that starting July 1, Medicare beneficiaries who are overweight or obese with qualifying conditions (BMI 27+ with cardiovascular disease or prediabetes, or BMI 35+ automatically) will be able to access GLP-1 weight loss drugs — Wegovy, Zepbound, and Foundayo — for a flat $50 monthly copay. The program runs as the 'Medicare GLP-1 Bridge' through December 2027 and was extended from six months because major insurers missed an April deadline to join a longer-term voluntary plan. The $50 copay does not count toward Part D deductible or the $2,100 annual out-of-pocket cap, and low-income subsidy holders cannot use Extra Help to offset it. Medicare has historically been barred from covering weight loss treatments. The $50 copay compares to cash prices of $199–$699 per month for the same drugs.

source.title: A New Medicare Option for Weight Loss Drugs: What Older Americans Should Know

payload.value: A $50 copay for a $500 drug sounds like access, but it is designed to work for the healthy Medicare beneficiary with disposable income — the sickest and poorest people the program is supposed to help are the most likely to drop out or never start.

source.title: A New Medicare Option for Weight Loss Drugs: What Older Americans Should Know

payload.value:
- $50/month is affordable for Medicare beneficiaries on fixed incomes: the median Medicare beneficiary lives on approximately $30,000 a year; $600 annually for a drug whose benefits disappear when you stop taking it is not a trivial burden for a third of the population the program targets.
- The Bridge is a stepping stone to permanent coverage: the Bridge program was specifically extended because not enough insurers signed up for the permanent program; the extension is a symptom of the permanent program's failure, not evidence of momentum toward it.
- The $50 copay will not count toward Part D limits, which is a minor technicality: for low-income beneficiaries who typically pay $5–$10 copays, a $50 copay is a 5-to-10x price increase for a drug they are told to take indefinitely.

source.title: A New Medicare Option for Weight Loss Drugs: What Older Americans Should Know

payload.value: The genuine tension is between making GLP-1 drugs available now — accepting that a flawed access program is better than no access — and waiting until a sustainable, equitable model exists that won't create a cliff effect when the Bridge ends in December 2027. The first path benefits the 14 million Medicare beneficiaries who can afford $50/month starting July. The second path protects against the predictable outcome where hundreds of thousands of patients start the drug, lose weight, then regain it when the program ends and they cannot afford the cash price. You cannot split this: a time-limited program that creates dependency is potentially more harmful than no program for the most vulnerable participants.
